## Synthesis: research report

**Question:** Research the competitive landscape for a proposed product: a web-based design tool that combines a Figma/Illustrator-style drag-and-drop canvas with AI-powered (Claude API) real-time generation of production-ready, semantic HTML5+CSS, a live preview pane, and a code editor panel — targeting designers who want to ship real static marketing websites without writing code. Positioned as faster/lower-friction than Webflow's learning curve and more code-transparent than typical no-code tools; secondary audience is developers wanting faster prototyping.

Research and compare these categories of similar/competing products (find current, real, up-to-date info via web search — do not rely on outdated knowledge):
1. AI-native design-to-code / prompt-to-app tools: v0.dev (Vercel), Bolt.new (StackBlitz), Lovable.dev, Onlook, Subframe, Replit Agent
2. Design-to-code conversion tools: Locofy.ai, Anima, TeleportHQ, Builder.io Visual Copilot
3. AI UI/UX design generators: Uizard, Visily, Framer AI
4. Established no-code website builders: Webflow, Framer (site builder side)
5. Design tools with code export: Figma Dev Mode + notable Figma-to-code plugins

For each product/company found: what it does, target user, how code generation actually works (deterministic templating vs LLM-generated), pricing tier if publicly known, and how it's similar to or different from the proposed tool (canvas-first design UX + live preview + AI codegen + code transparency).

End with a synthesis section: where is the actual gap or differentiation opportunity for a new entrant here, and what are the biggest risks (e.g. incumbents already converging on this exact feature set).

Output a well-organized markdown report with cited sources, suitable to check into a GitHub repository as a research document.

16 claims survived 3-vote adversarial verification. Merge semantic duplicates and synthesize.

## Confirmed claims
### [0] Onlook is a visual editor that edits React/Next.js code directly as the source of truth, rather than maintaining separate design files that need to be translated to code.
Vote: 3-0 · Source: https://www.onlook.com/ (primary)
Quote: "Because Onlook uses code as the source of truth, the types of designs you can create are unconstrained by Onlook's interface"
Verifier evidence (high): The claim is well-supported and consistently corroborated across multiple independent sources beyond just the primary marketing site. Onlook's own GitHub repo (github.com/onlook-dev/onlook) describes itself as an "Open-Source AI-First Design tool" that lets you "Visually build, style, and edit your React App with AI." Independent third-party coverage (LogRocket/DEV Community, itsfoss.com, ChatGate) all independently describe the same core mechanic: Onlook is a visual-first editor for React/Next.js where "code is the source of truth," changes made on the canvas write directly to the underlying React/JSX/Tailwind files (bi-directional sync — code edits also reflect in the visual canvas), rather than maintaining a separate proprietary design file format that gets exported/translated to code later. This is a verifiable, checkable architectural fact (the tool is open source and self-hostable, so the claim is falsifiable by inspecting the repo), not a vague or puffery marketing claim — and it's corroborated by independent technical writeups (LogRocket, itsfoss.com), not just the vendor's own site. No contradicting or qualifying evidence was found in the search results.

### [1] Onlook offers a free, self-hosted open-source version (available on GitHub) in addition to a paid cloud offering.
Vote: 3-0 · Source: https://www.onlook.com/ (primary)
Quote: "Onlook offers a free self-hosted version on GitHub and a paid cloud version."
Verifier evidence (high): The claim is directly supported by the primary source quote and independently corroborated by GitHub itself. The repo github.com/onlook-dev/onlook is described in its own title as "The Cursor for Designers • An Open-Source AI-First Design tool," is licensed Apache 2.0 (a genuine OSI open-source license, not source-available), has 17,652 stars, and has official docs pages titled "Development Setup – Running Locally" and "Cloud Deployment – Onlook Docs" (docs.onlook.com/self-hosting/cloud-deployment) that explicitly document self-hosting as a distinct path from cloud deployment. A search on Onlook's own pricing page corroborates: "Onlook can be self-hosted for free on GitHub. For the hosted cloud version, users need to contact their team or book a demo" — confirming both a free self-hosted OSS path and a separate paid/cloud offering (Free/Pro $25mo/Enterprise tiers on the cloud SaaS). Multiple independent sources (GitHub repo itself, Onlook's own docs site, Onlook's pricing page) all converge on the same fact, which is strong verification for a claim of this size (not an extraordinary claim — plenty of dev tools use this open-core self-host + paid-cloud model, e.g. Supabase, n8n, Plausible).

### [2] Onlook includes AI-powered generation/assistance where users can issue natural-language prompts (e.g. 'Design me an inventory tracker website') to have it build or modify the interface.
Vote: 3-0 · Source: https://www.onlook.com/ (primary)
Quote: "Users can request features like "Design me an inventory tracker website," with AI providing real-time help."
Verifier evidence (high): Onlook's own feature page (onlook.com/features/ai) is directly quoted by search results reproducing the exact example: "Design me an inventory tracker website for my Cafe" is shown as an AI prompt example, with the AI responding "Absolutely! Let's start by getting the general layout in place with a top navigation bar and a main content area." This matches the claim almost verbatim. Independent secondary sources (Onlook's GitHub repo description "Visually build, style, and edit your React App with AI", Y Combinator company page, and a BrightCoding review) corroborate that Onlook has a natural-language chat interface where users describe features/pages in plain English and the AI generates/edits real React+Tailwind code in response, with real-time code generation back into the codebase. No contradicting or qualifying source was found. The claim is a straightforward product-feature description (not an extraordinary claim), sourced primarily from the company's own site, which is appropriate source quality for this claim strength.

### [3] Lovable raised a $330 million Series B round at a $6.6 billion valuation, led by CapitalG and Menlo Ventures' Anthology fund
Vote: 3-0 · Source: https://lovable.dev/blog/series-b (primary)
Quote: "Raised: $330 million Series B; Valuation: $6.6 billion; Lead investors: CapitalG and Menlo Ventures' Anthology fund"
Verifier evidence (high): Claim fully corroborated by primary source (lovable.dev/blog/series-b) and independent journalism: TechCrunch ("Vibe-coding startup Lovable raises $330M at a $6.6B valuation") and CNBC ("Nvidia and Alphabet VC arms back vibe coding startup Lovable at $6.6 billion valuation") both confirm $330M Series B, $6.6B valuation, led by CapitalG and Menlo Ventures' Anthology fund. Multiple secondary sources (Yahoo Finance, SaaSRise, TheSaaSNews, Vestbee) repeat identical figures with no discrepancy. No contradicting reports found. Announcement dated June 22, 2026, so not outdated relative to current date (July 7, 2026).

### [4] Onlook is an open-source visual editor that lets users visually build, style, and edit React (Next.js + TailwindCSS) apps with AI, syncing canvas edits back to real source code, explicitly positioned as an alternative to Bolt.new, Lovable, V0, Replit Agent, Figma Make, and Webflow.
Vote: 3-0 · Source: https://github.com/onlook-dev/onlook (primary)
Quote: "an open-source alternative to Bolt.new, Lovable, V0, Replit Agent, Figma Make, Webflow"
Verifier evidence (high): WebFetch of github.com/onlook-dev/onlook confirms the README states verbatim: "An open-source alternative to Bolt.new, Lovable, V0, Replit Agent, Figma Make, Webflow, etc." Independent WebSearch corroborates this same phrase and title ("The Cursor for Designers • An Open-Source AI-First Design tool • Visually build, style, and edit your React App with AI"). The README also confirms the sync mechanism ("When the element is edited, we edit the element in our iFrame, then in code"), the Next.js + TailwindCSS + tRPC stack, and Apache 2.0 open-source license — all matching the claim precisely. No contradicting or qualifying sources found; this is a primary-source, self-description claim (not a third-party superlative claim), so the source quality matches the claim's strength.

### [5] Onlook's code generation is a hybrid of AI-chat-driven generation and direct visual DOM manipulation (drag-and-drop, Tailwind style toolbar), with instrumented code mapping DOM elements back to source for bidirectional editing -- not purely templated, not purely chat-only.
Vote: 3-0 · Source: https://github.com/onlook-dev/onlook (primary)
Quote: "visually build, style, and edit your React App with AI"
Verifier evidence (high): Official Onlook architecture docs (docs.onlook.com/developers/architecture) confirm: Onlook "finds the code, parses it into an AST, injects the styles, then writes it back," and "injects an attribute into the DOM elements at build-time that points back to the code like a sourcemap, and the attribute gives the location of the code block and the component scope" (data-oid attributes per DeepWiki analysis of the repo). This enables bidirectional sync: "changes in the visual editor instantly reflect in your codebase, and manual code edits immediately update the live preview." The GitHub README and product pages independently confirm both halves of the hybrid: (1) AI chat that "comprehends your entire project structure" and generates components from natural-language prompts, and (2) direct visual manipulation — click-to-select elements, drag to reposition, double-click to edit text, draw new divs, and a Tailwind-class toolbar for styling. Multiple independent sources (official docs, GitHub repo, LogRocket/DEV Community writeup, DeepWiki) converge on this same technical description with no contradictions found.

### [6] Claude Design supports building 'code-powered prototypes' (voice, video, shaders, 3D, built-in AI), showing Anthropic is not limiting this to static mockups but to interactive, code-backed output, encroaching on the proposed tool's live-preview/production-code value proposition.
Vote: 2-1 · Source: https://www.anthropic.com/news/claude-design-anthropic-labs (primary)
Quote: "Anyone can build code-powered prototypes with voice, video, shaders, 3D and built-in AI."
Verifier evidence (high): The quote is verified verbatim on the primary source (anthropic.com/news/claude-design-anthropic-labs): "Anyone can build code-powered prototypes with voice, video, shaders, 3D and built-in AI." Independent secondary sources (TechCrunch, VentureBeat, MacStories hands-on, DataCamp) corroborate the underlying facts: Claude writes real underlying code and renders it live ("a real thing to click through rather than a flat image"), the output is production-ready HTML/CSS/JS that is "real, runnable code... you can open in a browser, iterate on conversationally, and deploy," it includes a live preview with inline comments/direct edits/adjustment knobs, exports to standalone HTML files, and hands off to Claude Code for implementation. This directly substantiates the claim's core assertion — that Anthropic's own tool is not limited to static mockups but produces interactive, code-backed, live-previewed output — which does overlap with the proposed product's live-preview + production-code + code-transparency value proposition. Launch date confirmed as April 17, 2026 (TechCrunch, VentureBeat), so the claim is current (~3 months old as of July 7, 2026), not stale. Source quality (official company announcement, corroborated by multiple independent tech-press pieces) is sufficient for this claim's strength. One nuance for the report to note: Claude Design is conversational/comment-and-slider driven rather than a Figma-style drag-and-drop canvas, and targets a broader audience (non-designers, slides/one-pagers, general prototypes) than specifically "ship a static marketing website" — so the encroachment is real on the code/live-preview axis but only partial on the canvas-UX and narrow-use-case axis. This nuance doesn't refute the claim as worded, which is scoped specifically to the live-preview/production-code angle.

### [7] Claude Design runs on Anthropic's own most capable vision model (Claude Opus 4.7), meaning Anthropic is vertically integrating the exact 'Claude API-powered real-time generation' capability the proposed product would depend on purchasing via API — a platform-risk claim (the platform owner is also the competitor).
Vote: 3-0 · Source: https://www.anthropic.com/news/claude-design-anthropic-labs (primary)
Quote: "Claude Design is powered by our most capable vision model, Claude Opus 4.7."
Verifier evidence (high): The quote is accurate and verified against the primary source: Anthropic's official news page (anthropic.com/news/claude-design-anthropic-labs) states "Claude Design is powered by our most capable vision model, Claude Opus 4.7." This is independently corroborated by: (1) Anthropic's own official @claudeai X/Twitter announcement using near-identical wording ("Powered by Claude Opus 4.7, our most capable vision model"); (2) reputable tech press (TechCrunch, VentureBeat, 9to5Mac, TechRepublic) reporting the same launch and model pairing; (3) Anthropic's separate Opus 4.7 announcement (anthropic.com/news/claude-opus-4-7) and the AWS Bedrock blog confirming Opus 4.7's release and its improved vision/creative capabilities. Claude Design launched ~April 17, 2026 (per TechCrunch/9to5Mac) and has since received updates (design-system import, bidirectional Claude Code sync) as of reporting close to the current date (July 2026), so the claim is current, not stale. Claude Design explicitly supports exporting "standalone HTML files" and building prototypes conversationally, which substantiates the platform-risk framing: Anthropic is offering AI-driven design/code-generation output built on the same top-tier vision model (Opus 4.7) that a third party would otherwise access only via paid API — a legitimate vertical-integration/platform-risk concern for the proposed product. The only soft spot is that Claude Design's UX (conversational prompt-based) differs somewhat from the proposed product's canvas-first drag-and-drop paradigm, so "the exact capability" is a slight rhetorical overstatement, but the core factual claim (model, ownership, HTML output capability, platform risk) is well-supported by high-quality primary and secondary sources and not contradicted anywhere in search results.

### [8] Lovable raised a $330 million Series B round at a $6.6 billion valuation, led by CapitalG and Menlo Ventures with participation from Khosla Ventures, Salesforce Ventures, and Databricks Ventures.
Vote: 3-0 · Source: https://techcrunch.com/2025/12/18/vibe-coding-startup-lovable-raises-330m-at-a-6-6b-valuation/ (secondary)
Quote: "Lovable raises $330M at $6.6B valuation"
Verifier evidence (high): Multiple independent, credible sources corroborate the claim verbatim. TechCrunch (2025-12-18): "Vibe-coding startup Lovable raises $330M at a $6.6B valuation." CNBC: "Nvidia and Alphabet VC arms back vibe coding startup Lovable at $6.6 billion valuation." Fortune and Yahoo Finance confirm the same figures. Crucially, Menlo Ventures' own blog post (menlovc.com/perspective/software-creation-for-all-leading-lovables-330m-series-b/) is a primary source confirming Menlo led the round. Search results explicitly list the round as "led by CapitalG and Menlo Ventures' Anthology fund, with support from NVentures, Salesforce Ventures, Databricks Ventures, T.Capital, Atlassian Ventures, HubSpot Ventures, Khosla Ventures, DST Global, EQT Growth, Kinship Ventures, Accel, Creandum, and Evantic" — this confirms Khosla Ventures, Salesforce Ventures, and Databricks Ventures were indeed participants, matching the claim exactly. No contradicting evidence found; the claim is well-supported by both primary (investor's own blog) and multiple secondary (TechCrunch, CNBC, Fortune) sources, and is recent (Dec 2025, consistent with the July 2026 current date).

### [9] Lovable reached $100 million ARR within 8 months of launch and surpassed $200 million ARR four months later (by November 2025), indicating explosive growth in the AI/vibe-coding tool category.
Vote: 2-1 · Source: https://techcrunch.com/2025/12/18/vibe-coding-startup-lovable-raises-330m-at-a-6-6b-valuation/ (secondary)
Quote: "Reached $100 million ARR within 8 months of launch; Surpassed $200 million ARR four months later"
Verifier evidence (high): Corroborated by multiple independent, reputable sources beyond the TechCrunch secondary source cited. TechCrunch's own primary reporting (2025-07-23, "Eight months in, Swedish unicorn Lovable crosses the $100M ARR milestone") confirms the 8-month/$100M figure directly from company/investor disclosure. TechCrunch's follow-up (2025-11-19, "As Lovable hits $200M ARR...") and Bloomberg (2025-11-18, "Lovable Hits $200 Million ARR...announced at Slush 2025 in Helsinki") independently confirm the $200M ARR milestone in November 2025, four months after the $100M mark. Forbes (2025-07-23) independently characterized Lovable as "the fastest growing software startup ever," supporting the "explosive growth" framing. No contradicting or debunking coverage was found; skepticism identified in search results targets Lovable's code quality/emerging-markets strategy, not the revenue figures themselves. The claim's specific numbers (8 months to $100M, +4 months to $200M by Nov 2025) match the quote and are corroborated by at least three independent outlets (TechCrunch x2, Bloomberg) plus a supporting Forbes characterization, satisfying the bar for an extraordinary claim.

### [10] Subframe (a canvas-based design tool for React) generates code deterministically from the design canvas rather than via AI/LLM translation
Vote: 2-1 · Source: https://www.subframe.com/tips/best-visual-editors-react-tailwind (blog)
Quote: "code generation is deterministic, not AI-translated"
Verifier evidence (medium): The claim is supported not just by the cited marketing "tips" blog but corroborated by Subframe's own technical documentation at docs.subframe.com/concepts/design-to-code, which states directly: "Code generation in Subframe is deterministic and purely presentational (no API calls, state management, etc)." This is a more authoritative, non-marketing source (product docs) than the blog post cited, and it's internally consistent with the architecture described across multiple independent write-ups (Banani.co review, DesignWhine review): AI is used to help generate/place design elements, but the actual design-state-to-code export step is a deterministic compiler/mapping ("every layer maps directly to clean React and Tailwind CSS code"), not an LLM re-writing code from the design. No contradicting evidence was found in search — no reviewer or competitor source disputes this characterization or claims Subframe's export step uses an LLM to translate designs into code. The claim is current (searches return 2026 content, docs page is live) and is a mundane technical/architectural detail rather than an extraordinary claim, so self-reported documentation is adequate primary-source support, especially given cross-corroboration from a marketing blog, official docs, and third-party reviews all describing the same deterministic-export/AI-assists-design split.

### [11] Builder.io Visual Copilot uses a specialized AI model trained on over two million data points combined with the open-source Mitosis compiler to convert Figma designs into code across many frameworks.
Vote: 3-0 · Source: https://www.sixtythirtyten.co/blog/from-figma-to-code-ai-design-to-dev-workflows-in-2026 (blog)
Quote: "A specialized model trained on over two million data points transforms Figma structures into code hierarchies"
Verifier evidence (high): Builder.io's own official blog posts (builder.io/blog/figma-to-code-visual-copilot, builder.io/blog/ai-code-generation, builder.io/blog/visual-copilot-2) describe the exact same architecture claimed: "an initial model, trained with over 2 million data points, transforms flat design structures into code hierarchies," followed by the open-source Mitosis compiler converting the hierarchy into framework-specific code (React, Vue, Svelte, Angular, Qwik, Solid, HTML), with a final fine-tuned LLM pass for styling refinement. This is a primary-source-corroborated technical claim, not just marketing copy from the secondary blog being reviewed — the secondary source is accurately paraphrasing Builder.io's own public documentation. A 2026 search confirms this architecture description is still current (Visual Copilot's core pipeline is described as unchanged, with newer additions being ecosystem integrations like Fusion, not a different codegen mechanism).

### [12] Anima produces flat HTML structure with absolute/semi-absolute positioning that requires substantial refactoring before production use, positioning it for prototyping/presentations rather than shipping production code.
Vote: 3-0 · Source: https://sitegrade.io/en/blog/locofy-vs-builder-io-vs-anima-design-to-code-2026/ (blog)
Quote: "Weakness: Flat HTML structure requiring substantial refactoring before production use"
Verifier evidence (high): The claim is directly supported by the cited quote and independently corroborated by multiple sources. FigmaForge (figmaforge.io/anima-alternatives) states: "Anima converts Figma's visual layout to absolute CSS positioning — every element has top: 42px, left: 130px. This breaks on different screen sizes, is impossible to extend, and violates every accessibility and maintainability standard," describing it as "div soup." Anima's own support forum (forum.animaapp.com/t/auto-layout-from-figma-still-shows-absolute-positioning/229) confirms users hit this even with Figma auto-layout input. Anima's own blog (animaapp.com/blog/design-to-code/introducing-auto-flexbox) implicitly admits the problem existed: they built "Auto-Flexbox" specifically because "the code Anima generates uses absolute layout" by default and developers complained "the absolute layout makes the code not as helpful as it could be." A G2 review echoes the "requires cleanup" framing directly: "It's not a magic 'product-ready' button... users still spend some time cleaning up and adjusting the generated markup." This is a converging, multi-source (vendor's own admission + third-party comparison sites + user reviews + support forum) finding, not a single blog's cherry-picked claim, and it is current (sources dated 2026). The claim's framing — "requires substantial refactoring before production use, positioning it for prototyping/presentations rather than shipping production code" — is a reasonable, not overstated, synthesis of this evidence; if anything the corroborating sources are more blunt ("div soup," "no developer wants to maintain").

### [13] TeleportHQ's AI features generate layouts/components from natural language prompts (LLM-based generation), not purely deterministic templating, though output quality depends on design structure.
Vote: 2-1 · Source: https://makerstack.co/reviews/teleporthq-review/ (blog)
Quote: "You describe what you want in natural language and TeleportHQ generates a layout and components, which you can then edit visually or tune via additional prompts."
Verifier evidence (high): The claim holds up and is actually corroborated by a better source than the cited blog. TeleportHQ's own site has a page titled "AI Website builder powered by ChatGPT" (teleporthq.io/ai-website-builder-deprecated), and multiple independent reviews (kleap.co, durable.com, skywork.ai) consistently describe the same mechanism: "TeleportHQ's flagship feature is its AI website builder powered by ChatGPT technology, which uses ChatGPT to generate responsive website layouts based on text descriptions." This is a primary-source confirmation of LLM-based (not purely deterministic-template) generation — stronger evidence than the original makerstack.co blog citation alone. The newer "Copilot" feature is also described as LLM-driven: "Copilot provides conversational commands that transform natural language prompts into layout adjustments, text edits, or animation creation." The claim's hedge — "output quality depends on design structure/prompt clarity" — is echoed by reviewers noting "results depend heavily on prompt clarity." One nuance: the ChatGPT-powered builder page found is labeled "-deprecated" and there's a separate "AI website builder (Old version)" help article, suggesting TeleportHQ has iterated on/rebranded this feature over time (a "New TeleportHQ AI Website Builder" was announced), but all versions found are consistently described as LLM/prompt-based generation, not template-only. No source found disputes or contradicts LLM-based generation; no source claims the generation is purely deterministic templating.

### [14] TeleportHQ Professional tier is priced at $18/mo (or $9/mo billed annually), with Agency and Enterprise tiers at custom pricing and a 7-day free trial.
Vote: 3-0 · Source: https://makerstack.co/reviews/teleporthq-review/ (blog)
Quote: "Professional: $18/mo or $9/mo (annual)"
Verifier evidence (high): Verified directly against the primary source (https://teleporthq.io/pricing, fetched live). The official pricing page confirms: Professional Plan = $18/editor/month monthly, or $9/editor/month billed annually (50% savings) — exact match to the claim. It also confirms a free 7-day trial ("Trial Plan... 7 days from account activation, no credit card required") and a custom-priced upper tier ("Agency Plan — Custom pricing, contact required for quote"). The claim's wording "Agency and Enterprise tiers at custom pricing" is a very minor imprecision — the primary source's fetched summary shows one custom-priced tier named "Agency," not two separately named "Agency" and "Enterprise" tiers — but this does not contradict the substantive, checkable pricing figures ($18/$9) or the trial length (7 days), which are exactly right. Secondary sources (Findstack, SaaSWorthy) independently corroborate the $18 figure, though one WebSearch snippet cited a conflicting "€15/month billed yearly" figure from an older/cached version of the same page — the live fetch supersedes that as authoritative and current.

### [15] Builder.io Visual Copilot uses an AI model combined with the Mitosis compiler to convert Figma designs to code, supporting 8+ frameworks, and offers component mapping that links Figma components to existing codebase code
Vote: 3-0 · Source: https://www.aidesigner.ai/blog/figma-to-code-tools (blog)
Quote: "Uses AI model plus Mitosis compiler for conversion; supports 8+ frameworks"
Verifier evidence (high): Verified via Builder.io's own blog (primary source, not just the cited aidesigner.ai secondary blog). Builder.io's official posts (builder.io/blog/figma-to-code-visual-copilot, builder.io/blog/mitosis-get-started, builder.io/hub/demos/visual-copilot-component-mapping) confirm: (1) Mitosis + AI combo — "leverages AI models and an open-source compiler, Mitosis, to transform flat designs into code hierarchies, refined by an LLM"; (2) 8+ frameworks confirmed and actually exceeded — React, Vue, Svelte, Angular, Qwik, Solid, HTML, plus mobile SwiftUI, React Native, Flutter, Capacitor; (3) component mapping to existing codebase confirmed verbatim — "Visual Copilot uses AI to map reusable components in your Figma file to those in your code repository and generates code using your existing components when you have them." All three sub-claims in the quote are independently corroborated by Builder.io's own documentation, a first-party primary source stronger than the originally cited blog. No contradicting evidence found; feature (now branded partly as "Fusion") is current as of 2026 sources.


## Refuted claims (for transparency)
- "Lovable has strong usage scale, with 100,000+ new projects built daily and 25 million+ total projects created in its first year" (https://lovable.dev/blog/series-b, vote 0-3)
- "Anthropic itself now ships a canvas-based visual design tool with AI-powered code-generation and a direct handoff pipeline into Claude Code for implementation — the same combination of features (canvas design + AI codegen + code editor/build step) the proposed product is built around." (https://www.anthropic.com/news/claude-design-anthropic-labs, vote 1-2)
- "Locofy.ai produces live, code-backed interactive prototypes from designs rather than static code exports, using proprietary Large Design Models." (https://www.sixtythirtyten.co/blog/from-figma-to-code-ai-design-to-dev-workflows-in-2026, vote 1-2)
- "Across Builder.io, Locofy, and Anima, AI-assisted design-to-code conversion tools reach roughly 75% completion, still requiring developer refinement before production use." (https://www.sixtythirtyten.co/blog/from-figma-to-code-ai-design-to-dev-workflows-in-2026, vote 0-3)
- "Locofy, Builder.io, and Anima all use deterministic (template-based) code generation rather than LLM-generated code, mapping design layers to code output." (https://sitegrade.io/en/blog/locofy-vs-builder-io-vs-anima-design-to-code-2026/, vote 0-3)
- "Builder.io's design-to-code output has vendor lock-in tied to its proprietary SDK, functioning more as a headless CMS with design-to-code features than a pure conversion tool." (https://sitegrade.io/en/blog/locofy-vs-builder-io-vs-anima-design-to-code-2026/, vote 0-3)
- "Locofy uses a guided tagging system applied before code generation to improve semantic accuracy, focused primarily on React and Next.js output" (https://www.aidesigner.ai/blog/figma-to-code-tools, vote 0-3)
- "Most Figma-to-code tools (Anima, Locofy, Builder.io, TeleportHQ) produce only a rough starting point rather than production-ready output, typically requiring 20-40% manual refinement" (https://www.aidesigner.ai/blog/figma-to-code-tools, vote 0-3)
- "A case study describes a Figma-to-code plugin generating an onboarding flow that saved ~20 hours of boilerplate coding but required ~30 hours of refactoring, for a net loss of 10 hours." (https://figr.design/blog/figma-to-code-plugin, vote 0-3)

## Instructions
1. Identify claims that say the same thing — merge them, combine their sources.
2. Group related claims into coherent findings. Each finding should directly address the research question.
3. Assign confidence per finding: high (multiple primary sources, unanimous votes), medium (secondary sources or split votes), low (single source or blog-quality).
4. Write a 3-5 sentence executive summary answering the research question.
5. Note caveats: what's uncertain, what sources were weak, what time-sensitivity applies.
6. List 2-4 open questions that emerged but weren't answered.

Structured output only.

## Persistence

Switch: `/ponytail lite|full|ultra`.

## The ladder

Stop at the first rung that holds:

1. **Does this need to exist at all?** Speculative need = skip it, say so in one line. (YAGNI)

- dataviz: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".
- artifact-design: Design guidance and fundamentals for Artifacts.
- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.
- keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: "rebind ctrl+s", "add a chord shortcut", "change the submit key", "customize keybindings".
- verify: Verify that a code change actually does what it's supposed to by exercising it end-to-end and observing behavior — drive the affected flow, not just tests or typecheck. Run before committing nontrivial changes; bootstraps this repo's project verify skill if none exists yet. Don't invoke it on a diff that only touches tests, docs, or other code with no runtime surface to drive (a change to product source always has one) — there's nothing to observe.
- code-review: Review the current diff for correctness bugs and reuse/simplification/efficiency cleanups at the given effort level (low/medium: fewer, high-confidence findings; high→max: broader coverage, may include uncertain findings; ultra: deep multi-agent review in the cloud). Pass --comment to post findings as inline PR comments, or --fix to apply the findings to the working tree after the review.
- simplify: Review the changed code for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude cleanups, then apply the fixes. Quality only — it does not hunt for bugs; use /code-review for that.
- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.
- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo). Omit the interval to let the model self-pace. - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.
- schedule: Create, update, list, or run scheduled cloud agents (routines) that execute on a cron schedule. - When the user wants to schedule a recurring cloud agent, set up automated tasks, create a cron job for Claude Code, or manage their scheduled agents/routines. Also use when the user wants a one-time scheduled run ("run this once at 3pm", "remind me to check X tomorrow").
- claude-api: Reference for the Claude API / Anthropic SDK — model ids, pricing, params, streaming, tool use, MCP, agents, caching, token counting, model migration.

input.summary: The competitive landscape for a Figma-style canvas + live preview + Claude-API-powered semantic HTML/CSS codegen tool is crowded and consolidating fast, with the two most direct analogs — Onlook (open-source, canvas-first, code-as-source-of-truth React/Tailwind editor) and Anthropic's own Claude Design (code-powered, live-preview prototypes built on Opus 4.7) — already covering large parts of the proposed feature set. AI-native "vibe coding" tools (Lovable, v0, Bolt) have proven the category is enormous and investable (Lovable: $330M Series B at $6.6B valuation, $200M ARR within a year), but they are chat/prompt-first rather than canvas-first and mostly target React app scaffolding, not static marketing-site HTML/CSS shipping. Design-to-code conversion tools (Builder.io, Anima, TeleportHQ, Subframe) show two divergent codegen architectures already in production — deterministic/template compilers (Subframe, and Builder.io's AI-model-plus-Mitosis-compiler pipeline) versus LLM-generated markup with cleanup overhead (Anima's flat/absolute-positioned "div soup," TeleportHQ's ChatGPT-powered layout generation) — meaning the "LLM writes production-clean semantic HTML" claim is a real, not-yet-fully-solved differentiator if it can be delivered reliably. The single biggest strategic risk is platform/vertical-integration risk: Anthropic, the API vendor the proposed product would depend on, already ships a competing code-powered, live-preview, HTML-exporting design surface (Claude Design) built on its own flagship model, narrowing the window for a third party to build the same thing on top of Claude's API before Anthropic's first-party tool matures into direct overlap.

findings.claim: Onlook is the closest existing analog to the proposed product: an open-source, canvas-based visual editor for React/Next.js + Tailwind where code is the literal source of truth (not a separate design file translated to code), supports free self-hosting plus a paid cloud tier (Free/Pro $25/mo/Enterprise), lets users AI-prompt features in natural language (e.g. "Design me an inventory tracker website"), and generates code via a hybrid mechanism — an AI chat pass plus direct visual DOM manipulation (drag/drop, Tailwind style toolbar), with build-time sourcemap-like attributes bidirectionally linking canvas elements to AST-parsed code. It explicitly markets itself as "an open-source alternative to Bolt.new, Lovable, V0, Replit Agent, Figma Make, Webflow."
findings.evidence: Unanimous 3-0 verification across five constituent claims (code-as-source-of-truth, open-source self-host + paid cloud, AI natural-language prompting, explicit competitor positioning, hybrid AI+visual codegen mechanism). Corroborated by GitHub repo (17.6k stars, Apache 2.0), official architecture docs, and independent third-party writeups (LogRocket/DEV Community, itsfoss.com, DeepWiki). This is the single most feature-overlapping competitor found: canvas-first UX + AI codegen + code transparency + live sync are all present, though scoped to React/Next.js apps rather than static marketing-site HTML/CSS.

findings.claim: Lovable, the leading AI "vibe coding" app-builder, raised a $330 million Series B at a $6.6 billion valuation (Dec 2025/announced ~June 2026 per blog), led by CapitalG and Menlo Ventures' Anthology fund, with participation from Khosla Ventures, Salesforce Ventures, Databricks Ventures, NVentures, Atlassian Ventures, HubSpot Ventures, and others — demonstrating massive investor confidence in the AI-prompt-to-app category the proposed product sits adjacent to.
findings.evidence: Unanimous 3-0 verification, corroborated by primary company blog, investor's own blog (Menlo), and independent press (TechCrunch, CNBC, Fortune, Yahoo Finance) with no discrepancies. Signals the category (AI-generated web apps/sites) is well-capitalized and competitive, raising the bar for any new entrant's differentiation and speed to market.

findings.claim: Lovable reached $100M ARR within 8 months of launch and surpassed $200M ARR four months later (by November 2025) — one of the fastest revenue ramps ever recorded for a software startup.
findings.evidence: Verifier found strong corroboration (TechCrunch's own separate July and November 2025 reporting, Bloomberg, Forbes calling it "the fastest growing software startup ever") but the panel split 2-1, so confidence is capped at medium despite good evidence quality. Reinforces that end-user demand for AI-generated websites/apps is enormous and growing quickly, which cuts both ways for a new entrant: large market, but incumbents are scaling revenue extremely fast.

findings.claim: Anthropic now ships Claude Design, its own tool for building "code-powered prototypes" with live preview, voice/video/shaders/3D support, and exportable standalone HTML — running on Anthropic's own flagship vision model (Claude Opus 4.7) rather than being available only via the general Claude API. This is a direct platform-risk signal: the API vendor the proposed product depends on already ships an adjacent code-generation, live-preview product.
findings.evidence: Two related sub-claims: the code-powered-prototype/live-preview/HTML-export capability voted 2-1 (medium), while the Opus-4.7-powered vertical-integration/platform-risk claim voted 3-0 (high) with strong corroboration from TechCrunch, VentureBeat, 9to5Mac, TechRepublic, and Anthropic's own Opus 4.7 announcement. Important nuance flagged by the verifier: Claude Design is conversational/comment-and-slider driven, not a Figma-style drag-and-drop canvas, and targets a broader non-designer audience with slides/one-pagers/general prototypes rather than specifically shippable static marketing sites — so overlap is real on the code-transparency/live-preview axis but only partial on canvas-UX and narrow-use-case fit. A separate, more sweeping claim that Claude Design directly replicates the full proposed feature set (canvas + AI codegen + code editor + Claude Code handoff) was explicitly refuted by the verification panel (1-2).

findings.claim: Subframe, a canvas-based design tool for React/Tailwind, generates code deterministically (a compiler-style, non-AI translation step) rather than via LLM re-generation at export time — AI assists earlier in the design/placement flow, but the design-state-to-code mapping itself is a fixed, predictable transform.
findings.evidence: Verifier upgraded evidence quality by finding Subframe's own technical docs ("Code generation in Subframe is deterministic and purely presentational") plus corroboration from independent reviews (Banani.co, DesignWhine), but the panel vote was 2-1, capping confidence at medium. Relevant to the proposed product's architecture decision: a deterministic-mapping fallback (canvas state → templated HTML) may be more reliable/predictable than pure LLM generation, at the cost of flexibility.

findings.claim: Builder.io's Visual Copilot converts Figma designs to code using a specialized AI model (trained on 2M+ data points) combined with the open-source Mitosis compiler, supporting 8+ frameworks (React, Vue, Svelte, Angular, Qwik, Solid, HTML, plus mobile targets), and includes AI-driven component mapping that links Figma components to a user's existing codebase components rather than regenerating from scratch.
findings.evidence: Both constituent claims verified unanimously 3-0, with the verifier locating Builder.io's own primary-source blog posts confirming the exact architecture (AI model + Mitosis compiler + final LLM styling pass), framework count, and component-mapping/reuse feature. Shows a mature, well-funded incumbent already doing hybrid deterministic-compiler + AI-model codegen at production scale, one axis the proposed product would need to match or beat on output cleanliness. Note: a related claim that Builder.io's output has proprietary-SDK vendor lock-in was explicitly refuted (0-3).

findings.claim: Anima (Figma-to-code plugin) produces flat HTML with absolute/semi-absolute CSS positioning that requires substantial manual refactoring before production use, positioning it as a prototyping/handoff tool rather than a direct-to-production code generator.
findings.evidence: Unanimous 3-0, with converging evidence from a third-party comparison site, an independent competitor teardown ("div soup"), Anima's own user support forum, and even Anima's own blog implicitly admitting the problem (justifying its new "Auto-Flexbox" feature). This is a concrete, named failure mode (non-semantic, position-absolute markup) that the proposed product's semantic-HTML positioning could differentiate directly against, if it can reliably avoid it.

findings.claim: TeleportHQ generates layouts/components from natural-language prompts using an LLM (ChatGPT-powered builder plus a newer "Copilot" conversational editing feature) rather than purely deterministic templating, though output quality depends on prompt clarity/design structure; its Professional tier is priced at $18/mo (or $9/mo billed annually), with a custom-priced upper ("Agency") tier and a 7-day free trial.
findings.evidence: The pricing sub-claim verified unanimously 3-0 directly against TeleportHQ's live pricing page ($18/$9, 7-day trial, custom Agency tier confirmed). The LLM-generation sub-claim voted 2-1 (medium) despite the verifier finding TeleportHQ's own site confirming a "ChatGPT-powered" builder and consistent third-party corroboration (kleap.co, durable.com, skywork.ai) — capped at medium due to the split vote and the deprecated-page naming ambiguity. Establishes a low-cost ($9-18/mo) incumbent already doing LLM-prompt-to-website generation with visual editing, relevant as a pricing anchor.

input.caveats: Several refuted claims from the original research pass are worth flagging explicitly since they represent plausible-sounding but unverified narratives: (1) a claim that Anthropic's Claude Design is a direct, full-stack clone of the proposed feature set (canvas + AI codegen + code editor + build-step handoff) was refuted 1-2 — the more defensible finding is partial overlap on the code-transparency/live-preview axis only; (2) claims that Figma-to-code tools (Builder.io, Locofy, Anima) uniformly use deterministic-only generation, or conversely that they all hit a specific "~75% completion" or "20-40% manual refinement" benchmark, were refuted — treat any specific completion-percentage figures for this category as unverified; (3) Lovable's "100,000+ projects/day, 25M+ total projects" usage-scale claim was refuted and should not be cited. Time-sensitivity: Claude Design and Lovable's Series B are both very recent (April and December 2025/mid-2026 respectively) and this is a fast-moving space — pricing, funding, and feature sets for all listed tools should be re-verified before publication if this report is used more than ~1-2 months after 2026-07-07. Several sources are vendor blogs or single third-party review/comparison sites (makerstack.co, sixtythirtyten.co, sitegrade.io, aidesigner.ai) rather than primary documentation, which is why some findings are capped at medium confidence despite reasonable corroboration. No claims were independently verified about Uizard, Visily, Framer AI, Locofy.ai as a whole, Webflow, Figma Dev Mode, or Replit Agent — these categories from the original research brief returned no claims that survived 3-vote verification and are effectively uncovered gaps in this dataset (see open questions).
openQuestions: No verified data survived on Uizard, Visily, Framer AI (AI UI/UX generators), established no-code builders (Webflow, Framer sites), or Figma Dev Mode / Figma-to-code plugins — these categories from the original brief need a follow-up research pass since they are directly named as comparison targets.

How does the proposed product's specific claim of 'production-ready, semantic HTML5+CSS' (not React/JSX) differentiate it from Onlook, Builder.io, and Lovable, which all target component-framework output (React/Next.js/Tailwind) rather than plain static HTML/CSS for marketing sites — is static-HTML-first an underserved niche or a niche nobody wants because frameworks dominate?

What is Anthropic's actual roadmap intent for Claude Design — is it staying a general-purpose prototyping tool for non-designers, or is there any signal (job postings, changelog cadence, positioning language) that it will grow into a canvas-first, drag-and-drop design tool that would fully subsume the proposed product?

Among the deterministic-compiler tools (Subframe, Builder.io/Mitosis) versus LLM-generation tools (Anima, TeleportHQ), which approach actually produces cleaner semantic HTML for a *static marketing site* use case specifically (as opposed to app/component code) — none of the sources tested this narrower use case directly.
